A GPU Approach to Path Finding
Interesting, but it can be quite inefficient. Can't you just do dijkstra on the GPU? I guess it would be hard with simple OpenGL, but OpenCL should do the trick.

GPUs get their parallelism via SIMD: a single instruction operating on an array of many elements all at once. If a kernel/shader branches a lot, so that pieces of data must be acted upon individually, the GPU can't parallelize the work effectively. For example, Dijkstra's algorithm is queue oriented and isn't really amenable to parallel operation and a different approach must be taken to map the problem onto the target hardware.

But constructing a queue isn't entirely impossible on a GPU framework, it's just complicated and has some overhead. I'm just wondering how that would compare to the posted approach. Or, maybe the unnecessary work can somehow be culled in the opproach with cellular automata.

How is this any different from a straight forward breadth-first search? Ok, it has been implemented on a GPU, but otherwise?

At the risk of disrupting the circle-jerk, you should know that comments like these were among the "hyperbolic" ones posted. There is a longstanding precedent clearly indicating that such speech is not protected by the first amendment (Virginia v. Black). Yes, its true that "threats" that are obvious hyperbole are protected (Watts v. United States), the key work there is obvious. In the latter case, the young man on trial had witnesses that confirmed the context and nature of the "joke" to assassinate the president. But on the internet, you have no idea who is posting a comment or the state of mind that they are in.

Moreover these cases have only examined the conditions in which one might be convicted of a crime. The standard is much lower for prompting an investigation. If there indeed had been a threat, it would be essential to ensure that whoever was planning to assassinate a federal judge was not aware that they were being investigated; otherwise, they would have time to dispose of incriminating evidence, flee, or be all that much more determined to carry out their plans in a shorter timetable. No one should have to fear for their life, but particularly when one of the officials that represents our laws and way of life comes under fire, the integrity of the republic is put in jeopardy. It makes far more sense to be safe than sorry in this instance.

I'm all for free speech, but there are limits on what is acceptable and what warrants investigation. I believe that the governments actions in this case were completely justified.
